issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette: Kamran's eyes still glazed over when he recalled that fateful night on the train. He was working as a conductor when they hit a pedestrian on the tracks. The sound of screeching metal and the sight of blood pooling on the platform would be etched in his memory forever. In the aftermath, Kamran found himself increasingly on edge, unable to shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. It started with small things – he'd notice a passenger's bleeding cut and feel an overwhelming sense of unease, as if it was a harbinger of something worse to come. Or, when the air conditioning kicked in, dropping the cabin temperature just so, he'd be transported back to that night, his skin crawling with anxiety. These visual and tactile cues seemed to hijack his brain, catapulting him into a state of high alert. As time went on, Kamran's nervous system remained perpetually primed for disaster. He'd lie awake at night, listening for any unusual sounds outside his apartment, convinced that the slightest disturbance could signal an impending threat. His friends and family tried to reassure him, telling him he was safe, but Kamran just couldn't bring himself to believe it. Even when others told him everything would be alright, a voice in his head whispered otherwise. Kamran's inability to trust in his own safety soon began to seep into other areas of his life. He'd become hypervigilant on the job, constantly scanning the platforms and train cars for potential hazards. His colleagues started to notice a change in him – he was more irritable, always seeming to be "on edge." The irony wasn't lost on Kamran; as a conductor, it was his duty to ensure passenger safety, but now he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was just one misstep away from catastrophe. As the weeks turned into months, Kamran's relationships began to suffer. He stopped attending social gatherings, fearful of being trapped in a crowded space or confronted with some new, unforeseen danger. His occupation, once a source of pride and enjoyment, now felt like a minefield waiting to be navigated. It was this steady erosion of his personal and professional life that finally prompted Kamran to seek help – he couldn't keep living in a state of perpetual fear, constantly wondering when the other shoe would drop. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kamran confessed that what frightened him most was losing himself completely to this endless cycle of anxiety. He longed for the day when he could walk through a train station without his heart racing, or fall asleep at night without being haunted by visions of blood and twisted metal. The question was, how did he get back there?
